jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: The Shortcut
jokes.joke: I went to a hypnotherapist to cure my laziness. He said, 'Close your eyes. Imagine getting up at six, exercising, then working hard all day.' I said, 'Hang on. If you can put ideas in people's heads, why are we wasting this on me? My boss is right down the street.'

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Locker Room Mystery
jokes.joke: I joined a gym last month, and I still don’t understand the locker room. There’s a guy in there who’s been towel-drying the same knee for ten minutes. Ten minutes! Nobody’s knee is that wet. I’ve been going for weeks now, and he’s always there, always the knee. I don’t know who he is, but I know one thing: somewhere in this building, there’s a very clean knee, and a very dirty secret.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Unlocking the Mind
jokes.joke: I started seeing a hypnotherapist to cure my social anxiety, which is going great except he accidentally unlocked a past-life regression while I was halfway through changing into gym shorts. Now, instead of working out, I spend forty-five minutes every Tuesday sitting on a wooden bench, weeping silently while clutching a wet towel and remembering the exact moment I died at Gettysburg. The worst part is my gym membership still charges me a monthly maintenance fee for the emotional trauma.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Tile Mission
jokes.joke: So I finally saw a hypnotherapist about my laziness. He puts me under and says, 'From now on, you finish every single task you start.' I wake up feeling amazing. Then I walk into the bathroom. Two hours later my wife is banging on the door. Turns out I started counting the tiles… and there are a lot of tiles.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Password Clue
jokes.joke: I got locked out of my own email, and the recovery questions turned it into a mystery novel. It asked, 'What was your childhood nickname?' Apparently the answer wasn't 'I don't know, that's why I'm investigating.' By the third question I wasn't trying to regain access anymore, I was just trying to solve the cold case of who I used to be.

scores.comment: The obsessively towel-dried knee is a distinctive, amusing observation. Repetition builds curiosity, but the final 'dirty secret' is a familiar expression rather than a satisfying comic revelation. Stronger setup than payoff.

The Gettysburg regression creates an unexpected image, but the premise is convoluted and the joke takes too long to reach its destination. The maintenance-fee punchline feels disconnected from the central absurdity and produces little comic payoff.

A coherent comic reversal: curing laziness creates an even less productive compulsion. The bathroom reveal provides effective escalation, although counting tiles is a relatively mild payoff. Clean construction and believable stage delivery.

Relatable frustration transformed into a clever identity mystery. The childhood-nickname response is the strongest laugh, while the cold-case ending supplies a satisfying thematic callback. Concise, natural delivery, though the final turn is more witty than laugh-inducing.
Clear premise and a tidy pivot to the boss, but the final line’s logic is a bit ambiguous and the boss target is familiar.
The image of weeping on a bench, clutching a towel and remembering Gettysburg is funny, but the setup is overloaded and the maintenance-fee closer is weaker than the middle.
Strong turn: the hypnosis works too literally and traps him counting bathroom tiles. Clean rhythm, and the last line lands the laugh.
Relatable account-recovery frustration with a decent ‘cold case of who I used to be’ closer, but the nickname exchange is muddled and the turn is somewhat expected.
Solid and competent redirection to the boss, though a bit structurally predictable.
Great observational detail with a strong, clean callback and a punchy final line.
Nice commitment to the literal interpretation of finishing tasks with a funny bathroom escalation.
Clever spin on password recovery with a strong philosophical punchline at the end.
Clear premise and clean delivery, but the boss redirect is the most obvious available turn and lands soft.
Strong observational escalation and a sharp final image that actually carries the laugh.
Premise works but Gettysburg past-life is familiar and the membership-fee closer is weak.
Tight first-person setup with a satisfying shift from recovery questions to cold-case investigation.
Clear premise and payoff; boss redirection is mildly funny but fairly familiar.
Strong observational setup with a specific image and a neat mystery-style tag at the end.
Readable and specific, but overlong and the final fee joke is weaker than the setup.
Clean stand-up structure and escalation; tile-counting payoff is solid but not especially unexpected.
